claims.claim: The reviewer says Dread Trident's audience appears to be literary studies scholars.
claims.source: Adrianna Burton, 'Book Review: Dread Trident', Analog Game Studies, 2022
claims.quote: audience appears to be literary studies scholars

claims.claim: Carbonell says role-playing gametexts appeared to him an overlooked area of investigation for literary scholars.
claims.source: Curtis D. Carbonell, interviewed on the Liverpool University Press blog, 2020
claims.quote: an overlooked area of investigation for literary scholars

claims.feature: other: close reading of game texts
claims.claim: Carbonell says he began close readings of the archives of published role-playing material.
claims.source: Curtis D. Carbonell, interviewed on the Liverpool University Press blog, 2020
claims.quote: I then began my close readings of the archives

claims.claim: Carbonell disputes the view that role-playing material has been overlooked for its simplicity or lack of textual and psychological depth.
claims.source: Curtis D. Carbonell, interviewed on the Liverpool University Press blog, 2020
claims.quote: because of its simplicity or lack of textual and psychological depth

claims.claim: Carbonell says forty years of published role-playing material was waiting to be mined by a literary scholar.
claims.source: Curtis D. Carbonell, interviewed on the Liverpool University Press blog, 2020
claims.quote: forty years of published material was out there, waiting to be mined

claims.claim: Carbonell calls D&D exemplary of the middle ground where literary tropes push up against game mechanics.
claims.source: Curtis D. Carbonell, interviewed on the Liverpool University Press blog, 2020
claims.quote: where we see literary tropes push up against game mechanics

claims.claim: A reviewer reports Carbonell arguing that Lovecraft's impulse to categorise in rich description is reflected in early TRPGs.
claims.source: Clare Wall, 'Review of Dread Trident', SFRA Review 52.1, 2022
claims.quote: an impulse which Carbonell argues is also reflected in early TRPGs

claims.claim: Noonan reports that a DM reading boxed text holds player attention for two sentences and no further.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: If you’re the DM, you get two sentences. Period.

claims.claim: Noonan's hypothesis was that boxed text longer than a paragraph probably is not worth reading aloud.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: boxed text longer than a paragraph probably isn’t worth reading

claims.claim: Noonan observed players repeatedly missing the actual data inside the boxed text, such as room dimensions and exits.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: players were missing the actual data in the boxed text

claims.claim: Noonan's mechanism for the failure is that boxed text replaces the game's conversation with oration.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: Boxed text replaces that conversation with oration

claims.claim: Noonan holds that at its heart a D&D game is a conversation.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: At its heart, a D&D game is a conversation

claims.claim: Noonan concludes that oration is inherently harder to concentrate on than conversation.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: oration is inherently harder to concentrate on than conversation

claims.claim: Noonan notes DMs are by and large reading the boxed text cold, from a script never uttered aloud before.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: DMs are, by and large, reading the boxed text cold

claims.claim: Writing in 2005, the authors say boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer than it was then.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: used to be a lot longer than it is today
